question: Resistance from a medium-voltage arrester’s ground terminal to the ground system shall be:
choices: Less than 0.5 Ω
Less than 25 Ω
At least 100 MΩ
Equal to the arrester’s watts-loss
explanation: ATS 7.19.2.D.3 says less than 0.5 Ω, and it still points at the grounding section. 25 Ω is the NEC supplemental-rod idea, not this bond. Watts-loss is a separate comparison.

question: Watts-loss on a substation arrester is judged by:
choices: A single watt limit printed for every class
Comparison with similar units and the test-set data
Table 100.7
The recloser’s vacuum pressure
explanation: 7.19.2.D.4 evaluates watts-loss against similar arresters and the test equipment manufacturer’s data. A lone number with no twin and no baseline is not that test.

question: Two station arresters of the same rating show very different watts-loss, and the manufacturer published nothing. ATS 7.19.2 says:
choices: Pass both if insulation resistance is high
Compare them with each other and with the test-set data
Apply Table 100.6 VLF
Ignore watts; only the 0.5 Ω ground lead matters
explanation: Watts-loss is a comparison, not a single watt cap in that paragraph. The ground lead still has its own 0.5 Ω screen. A high megohm does not explain a watts outlier.

question: When a liquid-filled transformer has surge arresters, ATS 7.2.2.B.17 says to test them:
choices: In accordance with section 7.19
By a dissolved-gas sample of the arrester
At the VLF cable voltage
Only if they are gapped silicon carbide
explanation: The transformer section does not invent a private arrester test. It sends you to 7.19. The arrester result is then judged by 7.2.2.D.17, which points back at that same section.

question: ATS 7.19.2 wants the ground lead on each medium-voltage arrester:
choices: Daisy-chained through the next arrester
Individually attached to ground, as short as practical
Left off until the watts-loss test
Fused at the size in the cable study
explanation: Each arrester gets its own ground lead, kept short. Fuse size is a switch and coordination check, not this arrester inspection. The ground terminal to the ground system is then a resistance test, held under 0.5 ohm.

question: With no manufacturer insulation value, ATS 7.19.2 insulation resistance of a surge arrester is judged by:
choices: A fixed 1,000 megohm floor for every voltage
Table 100.1
Table 100.7 trip time
The recloser vacuum limit
explanation: The test is phase terminal to ground. No manufacturer number means Table 100.1, and a value under that table is investigated. A memorized 100, 10, or 1 megohm is not what the paragraph prints.

question: Watts-loss on a substation arrester, ATS 7.19.2, is accepted by:
choices: Comparing similar units and the test-set data
A single watt value printed for every class
The oil power-factor table
A turns-ratio limit of 0.5 percent
explanation: There is no universal watt ceiling in that test-value line. You compare like units and the instrument data. The ground connection is the separate 0.5 ohm check.

question: A new station-class arrester has a surge counter. During acceptance inspection, you:
choices: Reset the counter to zero
Make sure it is correctly mounted and connected, and record its reading
Remove it, since it adds impedance to the ground lead
Bypass it during the insulation test only
explanation: The ATS visual list includes verifying the stroke counter is correctly mounted and electrically connected, and recording its reading. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.19.2.A.7 and A.8.

question: Which arrester acceptance test is called for on substation-class arresters specifically?
choices: Watts-loss
Dc hipot at twice rating
Turns ratio
Contact resistance across the arrester
explanation: ATS lists a watts-loss test for substation-class arresters, judged by comparison with similar units and the test-set maker's data. The insulation-resistance and ground-connection tests apply to every medium- and high-voltage arrester. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.19.2.B.4 and D.4.

question: Besides the ground-terminal-to-ground-system resistance, how is the arrester's grounding connection tested at acceptance?
choices: It is not; only visual inspection applies
In accordance with the grounding-system section of ATS
With a 5 kV insulation test
With a clamp-on meter only
explanation: The arrester section sends you to the grounding-systems section for the ground connection test, and the ground terminal to ground system must read under 0.5 Ω. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.19.2.B.3 and D.3; 7.13.

question: On a metal-oxide arrester nameplate, MCOV means:
choices: The highest rms voltage it may see continuously
The crest voltage across the arrester during a lightning discharge
The voltage at which the arrester first conducts 1 mA
The rms voltage the arrester can withstand for a 10-second overvoltage
explanation: C62.11 defines maximum continuous operating voltage as the highest rms power-frequency voltage designated for continuous application between the terminals. Discharge voltage is what appears during surge current. Source: IEEE C62.11-2020, 3.1 (maximum continuous operating voltage).

question: An older arrester spec lists a duty-cycle voltage rating. What does IEEE C62.11-2020 say about that rating?
choices: It is the same thing as MCOV
It is historical and being phased out
It is the minimum discharge voltage
It has replaced MCOV as the main rating used for selection
explanation: C62.11-2020 describes the duty-cycle rating as historical, suited to the previous generation of arresters, and being removed. MCOV is the continuous rating used with modern metal-oxide arresters. Source: IEEE C62.11-2020, 3.1 (duty-cycle voltage rating).

question: Under NFPA 780, what nominal discharge current rating must the service-entrance SPD have?
choices: At least 3 kA per phase
At least 200 kA total
20 kA or more per phase (8/20 µs wave)
At least 10 kA (10/350 µs) total
explanation: A lightning-protected structure needs an SPD at every power service, built into or right next to the service equipment. Size it for a nominal discharge current of 20 kA or more on each phase, using the 8/20 µs wave. Source: NFPA 780-2026, 4.19.2.1 and 4.19.2.5 to 4.19.2.7.

question: Besides the service, where else does NFPA 780 require SPDs on power circuits?
choices: At every receptacle
Only at the generator
Where feeders or branch circuits enter or leave the building to another building over runs longer than 100 ft (30 m)
Nowhere else
explanation: Long runs between buildings pick up surge energy, so SPDs go where those circuits enter or leave when the run is over 100 ft. There is an exception, under engineering supervision, when the threat is negligible or equal protection exists. Source: NFPA 780-2026, 4.19.2.2 and 4.19.2.4.
